title: Ghost-Type Hunting Secrets
content:
Ghost hunting is about timing and confidence in the route. Shadow Marsh can produce valuable checks, but only when the player knows where the useful rooms are and can reset without draining resources. Random full clears are the fastest way to make ghost farming feel worse than it is.

Shados is the practical learner because it lets you understand the route. Shadowclaw is the higher-value target once the path is stable. Ghost Veil should support the dangerous window or repeated check loop, not the first trip into the marsh.

If ghost farming feels unlucky, check the route before blaming the odds. A short loop with several clean attempts is better than one dramatic clear that takes too long to repeat.
image_alt: Ghost-Type Hunting Secrets guide image
answer: Ghost hunting works best when Shadow Marsh is reduced to a short repeatable loop. Use Shados to learn the route, target Shadowclaw once the path is stable, and save Ghost Veil for the dangerous or repeated check window.
steps: Scout Shadow Marsh without Ghost Veil first.
Use Shados to learn ghost-route pressure and safe reset points.
Target Shadowclaw only after the path is repeatable.
Cut side rooms that do not support the ghost check.
Use Ghost Veil for the section that decides the attempt.
Keep one support slot for status or survival problems.
Track attempts rather than relying on one long clear.
If runs feel unlucky, shorten the route before spending more buffs.
recommended_setup: Route learner: Shados for safe ghost-route practice.
Target: Shadowclaw once the loop is stable.
Support slot: durability or status coverage for Marsh pressure.
Recipe: Ghost Veil for the meaningful danger window.
Route style: short checks, clean resets, repeated attempts.
Best use: players farming ghost targets without wasting rare buffs.
common_mistakes: Full-clearing Shadow Marsh when the ghost check happens earlier.
Using Ghost Veil before learning the route.
Targeting Shadowclaw before normal encounters are stable.
Ignoring status pressure that quietly ruins the loop.
Switching targets after a few attempts instead of improving reset timing.
Treating one long clear as better than multiple short checks.

faqs.question: What is the best ghost farming route?
faqs.answer: A short Shadow Marsh loop that reaches the useful ghost check quickly and resets cleanly.

faqs.question: Should I start with Shados or Shadowclaw?
faqs.answer: Start with Shados to learn the route. Farm Shadowclaw once the route is stable.

faqs.question: When does Ghost Veil help ghost hunting?
faqs.answer: Use Ghost Veil when ghost pressure is the route problem and the target section is already mapped.

faqs.question: Why does ghost farming feel slow?
faqs.answer: The route is too long when side rooms lower useful checks per hour. Cut optional rooms first.

faqs.question: Do I need a support Pokemon?
faqs.answer: Usually yes. Status and survival support can matter more than another attacker in Shadow Marsh.

faqs.question: How many ghost runs should I compare?
faqs.answer: Compare several runs with the same night or weather condition before changing the team. Ghost routes vary heavily by timing.

faqs.question: Should Ghost Veil and bait be used together?
faqs.answer: Only when the ghost route is stable. If the team struggles to reach the target section, fix survival before adding bait.

faqs.question: When should a ghost hunt end?
faqs.answer: End after the ghost check and any planned dark-side pickup. Long side rooms weaken ghost farming value.

title: Electric-Type Speed Demon Build
content:
Electric speed teams should win by reducing downtime, not by pretending every route is a race. Zaprat gives early electric pressure, Mechabit adds utility when the route fights back, and Voltscale becomes the high-value carry once the team can support it.

Speed Potion is strongest on a route that already has clean movement and predictable fights. If the path is messy, the potion only makes the mistakes happen faster. Thunder Arena and Windmill Plains reward speed when the team has enough control to turn that speed into more useful attempts.

Build the team around the bottleneck. If opening fights are slow, change the lead. If the route collapses halfway through, add utility. If travel is the real problem, shorten the loop before spending recipes.
image_alt: Electric-Type Speed Demon Build guide image
answer: Electric speed builds work when speed reduces downtime. Use Zaprat for early pressure, Mechabit for utility, Voltscale as the high-value carry, and Speed Potion only on clean repeatable routes.
steps: Identify whether the route needs faster fights, shorter travel, or more stability.
Use Zaprat for early electric tempo.
Add Mechabit when utility and durability matter.
Use Voltscale as the carry once the route can support it.
Scout the loop before using Speed Potion.
Use Speed Potion only when it increases useful attempts, not just movement speed.
Keep one backup for bad openings or resistant matchups.
Adjust the bottleneck first instead of stacking more speed blindly.
recommended_setup: Early pressure: Zaprat lead for simple electric tempo.
Utility slot: Mechabit when route pressure needs control.
Carry: Voltscale for high-value electric-dragon routes.
Recipe: Speed Potion on known loops with low downtime.
Optional damage: Thunder Strike when a specific room needs burst.
Best use: Thunder Arena, Windmill Plains, and any route where clean speed increases attempts.
common_mistakes: Using Speed Potion on a route that is still messy.
Building only speed and no backup plan.
Ignoring resistant matchups that slow electric teams down.
Treating Voltscale as an early shortcut before the route can support it.
Adding more speed when utility or survival is the real bottleneck.
Measuring one fast clear instead of repeated useful attempts.

faqs.question: What is the biggest mistake in Electric team builds?
faqs.answer: Filling every slot with Electric type Pokemon instead of covering type weaknesses. A good electric team needs defensive backup, utility roles, and coverage for resistances that pure Electric typing cannot handle. Check the related habitat pages for Pokemon that complement your core without breaking the type theme.

faqs.question: What makes an electric speed build good?
faqs.answer: It turns speed into more useful attempts, not just faster movement.

faqs.question: Who should lead?
faqs.answer: Zaprat is the simple early lead. Voltscale is better once the route can support a stronger carry.

faqs.question: When does Speed Potion support an electric build?
faqs.answer: Use Speed Potion when the electric team already clears safely and needs more attempts per session, especially in open routes.

faqs.question: Is Mechabit too slow for this build?
faqs.answer: No. Mechabit can be the utility slot that keeps a fast route from collapsing.

faqs.question: Why is my speed team inconsistent?
faqs.answer: It likely has speed without stability. Add coverage or utility before adding more tempo.

faqs.question: What recipes work best with Electric teams?
faqs.answer: Electric teams work best with recipes that boost the team's primary role. Damage-oriented Electric teams benefit from burst or damage buff recipes. Defensive teams need sustain and armor recipes. Check the recipe page for buffs that align with your team's specific role composition.

faqs.question: How many Electric Pokemon do I need before starting this build?
faqs.answer: Start the build when you have 3 confirmed Electric Pokemon with different roles (Tank, Attacker, Support or similar). The remaining slots should cover type weaknesses and provide utility. Commit to a full electric build only after the core is stable.

title: How to Unlock Dragon's Den
content:
Dragon's Den should be treated as a commitment route. It asks for unlock preparation, late-game durability, and a team that can survive long enough for dragon pressure to matter. Entering just because the name sounds exciting usually turns into wasted recipes.

Voltscale and Snorizard are the practical planning anchors, while Primordion belongs to the late-game version of the route. Dragon's Fury should be reserved for the section that decides the run, not the first room. If you cannot reach that section consistently, the team is not ready.

The clean unlock plan is simple: prepare in supporting habitats, scout the den cheaply, then bring the serious recipe setup after you know the path. Dragon's Den rewards patience more than improvisation.
image_alt: How to Unlock Dragon's Den guide image
answer: Unlock Dragon's Den only after supporting routes are stable. Build around Voltscale, Snorizard, or Primordion depending on progress, and save Dragon's Fury for the section that actually decides the run.
steps: Stabilize supporting dragon or late-game routes before entering the den seriously.
Scout Dragon's Den once without rare recipes.
Use Voltscale when electric-dragon pressure helps the route.
Use Snorizard when durability matters more than speed.
Treat Primordion as a late-game target, not an early route fix.
Identify the section where Dragon's Fury changes the outcome.
Use Dragon's Fury only on serious attempts after the path is known.
If the team cannot reach the key room, improve backup support before trying again.
recommended_setup: Carry option: Voltscale for tempo and pressure.
Durable option: Snorizard for long-route stability.
Late-game target: Primordion once the route is properly supported.
Recipe: Dragon's Fury for the decisive room or check.
Backup: one stabilizer that prevents the run from failing before the dragon window.
Best use: late-game unlock planning and serious dragon-route attempts.
common_mistakes: Entering Dragon's Den before support routes are stable.
Using Dragon's Fury on the first scouting run.
Building only damage and failing before the key room.
Treating Primordion as a shortcut instead of a late-game target.
Ignoring travel and recovery cost.
Repeating the same failed attempt without changing backup support.

faqs.question: What blocks Dragon's Den attempts?
faqs.answer: Dragon's Den attempts fail when the unlock route is treated like a normal farming loop. Prepare the team for the gate section first.

faqs.question: When should I attempt Dragon's Den?
faqs.answer: Attempt it seriously after supporting routes are stable and your team can reach the key section without heavy recovery.

faqs.question: Which Pokemon should I build around?
faqs.answer: Use Voltscale for pressure, Snorizard for durability, and Primordion for late-game planning.

faqs.question: When should I use Dragon's Fury?
faqs.answer: Use it on the decisive section after you know the route, not during blind scouting.

faqs.question: Why does Dragon's Den feel too expensive?
faqs.answer: The team cannot reach the important section consistently yet. Improve support before spending more recipes.

faqs.question: Is this a farming route?
faqs.answer: Not at first. Treat it as an unlock and scouting route before turning it into a repeatable farm.

faqs.question: How should I prepare for Dragon's Den?
faqs.answer: Confirm the route entry, support slot, and Dragon's Fury timing before committing rare materials to repeated attempts.

faqs.question: When should I postpone Dragon's Den?
faqs.answer: Postpone it when the team cannot reach the important section consistently. More recipes will not fix an unstable entry route.

title: Beginner's Guide to Training Grounds
content:
Training Grounds is where players should learn team roles before spending rare resources elsewhere. It is not glamorous, but it teaches the habits that make harder routes cheaper: lead choice, backup timing, food use, recipe discipline, and when to reset.

Bulbin is the easiest role teacher because it keeps early mistakes manageable. Tidlet gives a low-risk neutral backup, while Thornvine helps players practice grass pressure without jumping into harsher habitats. Grass Heal should be used as a learning tool only after you understand which part of the route causes trouble.

Do not leave Training Grounds just because you can clear it once. Leave when you can explain why your lead works, why your backup exists, and what recipe timing would improve the next route.
image_alt: Beginner's Guide to Training Grounds guide image
answer: Training Grounds is the best place to learn team roles, not just gain early wins. Use Bulbin, Tidlet, and Thornvine to practice stable routing before spending rare recipes in harder habitats.
steps: Use Training Grounds to test one team idea at a time.
Start with Bulbin if you need a forgiving lead.
Add Tidlet when you want a safe neutral backup.
Use Thornvine to practice grass pressure and beginner farming.
Run the route without rare recipes first.
Use Grass Heal only after you know where the route becomes risky.
Practice changing one variable per run: lead, backup, food, or recipe timing.
Move on when you understand the role of each slot, not just when you get one clear.
recommended_setup: Lead: Bulbin for forgiving early role practice.
Backup: Tidlet for safe neutral recovery from bad openings.
Pressure pick: Thornvine for simple grass-route practice.
Recipe: Grass Heal after the problem section is identified.
Route style: repeatable tests with one change at a time.
Best use: new players learning how teams and recipes actually affect routes.
common_mistakes: Leaving Training Grounds before understanding team roles.
Using rare recipes just to win practice fights.
Testing too many Pokemon at once.
Judging a team from one clear instead of repeated attempts.
Ignoring backup timing because the route is easy.
Skipping food and recipe habits that matter later.

faqs.question: What should beginners avoid in Training Grounds?
faqs.answer: Beginners should avoid treating Training Grounds like a permanent farm. Use it to test roles, then move to real habitats once the basics are stable.

faqs.question: Why should I use Training Grounds?
faqs.answer: It teaches team roles and route habits without the cost of harder habitats.

faqs.question: Which Pokemon should beginners test?
faqs.answer: Bulbin, Tidlet, and Thornvine give a simple spread of stability, backup safety, and pressure.

faqs.question: Should I use recipes here?
faqs.answer: Use cheap or relevant recipes only after you know what problem they are meant to solve.

faqs.question: When am I ready to leave?
faqs.answer: When you can explain your lead, backup, recipe timing, and reset point clearly.

faqs.question: Is Training Grounds only for new players?
faqs.answer: No. It is also useful when testing a new team shape before taking it into expensive routes.

faqs.question: How long should I stay in Training Grounds?
faqs.answer: Stay until starter role, backup support, and recipe timing feel predictable. After that, Forest Valley or Crystal Lake gives better route practice.

faqs.question: When is Training Grounds still useful later?
faqs.answer: Return later when testing a new team shape or recipe timing without risking a harder habitat run.

title: Poison-Type Team Analysis
content:
Poison teams win by control, not by racing every encounter. Venomleaf gives the team its basic identity, while Leafon supports longer pressure routes where grass and poison value overlap. Nightmare Forest and similar habitats reward poison teams that can survive long fights and control bad openings.

Ghost Veil or poison-support recipes should be used when the route contains dangerous status or dark pressure, not as a default opener. If the team is slow, first check whether it lacks finishing power or whether the route is simply too long.

A good poison team should make hard sections feel predictable. It should not turn every run into a slow damage-over-time experiment with no clear payoff.
image_alt: Poison-Type Team Analysis guide image
answer: Poison teams are control teams. Use Venomleaf for core pressure, Leafon for longer grass-poison routes, and Ghost Veil only when the route has a dangerous control or survival window.
steps: Use Venomleaf as the core poison-pressure pick.
Add Leafon when the route rewards longer grass-poison control.
Scout the target habitat before committing Ghost Veil.
Keep one slot for finishing power so fights do not drag forever.
Use Ghost Veil when dark or ghost-style pressure threatens the route.
Shorten routes that turn poison damage into unnecessary downtime.
Review whether failures come from survival, speed, or lack of finishing power.
Farm Nightmare Forest-style routes only after normal clears become predictable.
recommended_setup: Core: Venomleaf for poison pressure.
Control support: Leafon for longer grass-poison routes.
Finisher: one damage slot to prevent slow clears.
Recipe: Ghost Veil for dangerous control windows.
Route fit: Nightmare Forest and other pressure-heavy habitats.
Best use: players who prefer stable control over burst racing.
common_mistakes: Building poison teams with no finisher.
Using Ghost Veil before finding the dangerous section.
Letting damage-over-time make routes slower than necessary.
Entering hard control routes before normal clears are predictable.
Ignoring grass-poison overlap on Leafon.
Changing the whole team when only the finishing slot is weak.

faqs.question: What is a poison team good at?
faqs.answer: It is good at controlling hard routes and making dangerous sections predictable.

faqs.question: Who is the main poison pick?
faqs.answer: Venomleaf is the core pressure pick, while Leafon supports longer grass-poison routes.

faqs.question: Does a poison team need Ghost Veil?
faqs.answer: Use Ghost Veil only when the route also has ghost pressure. Poison teams usually need status control before ghost-specific support.

faqs.question: Why is my poison team slow?
faqs.answer: It may lack finishing power or be running routes that are too long for poison control to pay off.

faqs.question: Where should I use poison teams?
faqs.answer: They fit pressure-heavy habitats such as Nightmare Forest-style routes once normal clears are stable.

faqs.question: What is the biggest mistake in Grass/Poison team builds?
faqs.answer: Filling every slot with Grass/Poison type Pokemon instead of covering type weaknesses. A good grass/poison team needs defensive backup, utility roles, and coverage for resistances that pure Grass/Poison typing cannot handle. Check the related habitat pages for Pokemon that complement your core without breaking the type theme.

faqs.question: What recipes work best with Grass/Poison teams?
faqs.answer: Grass/Poison teams work best with recipes that boost the team's primary role. Damage-oriented Grass/Poison teams benefit from burst or damage buff recipes. Defensive teams need sustain and armor recipes. Check the recipe page for buffs that align with your team's specific role composition.

faqs.question: How many Grass/Poison Pokemon do I need before starting this build?
faqs.answer: Start the build when you have 3 confirmed Grass/Poison Pokemon with different roles (Tank, Attacker, Support or similar). The remaining slots should cover type weaknesses and provide utility. Commit to a full grass/poison build only after the core is stable.

title: All 4 Legendary Pokemon Locations
seo_title: Pokopia Legendary Locations Guide
seo_description: Find legendary Pokemon locations in Pokopia, including Flamexor, Voltscale, Shadowclaw, Primordion, route prep, and Lucky Charm timing.
content:
Legendary locations should be approached as route projects. Flamexor, Voltscale, Shadowclaw, and Primordion are exciting targets, but each one is tied to a different kind of preparation. The mistake is treating all legendary hunts as the same Lucky Charm session.

Volcanic Cave rewards fire-route preparation for Flamexor. Thunder Arena asks for tempo before Voltscale attempts. Shadow Marsh needs a short ghost loop before Shadowclaw farming. Primordion belongs to the late-game planning bucket and should not be treated as a casual early detour.

Scout each location cheaply, then decide whether the route is ready for real attempts. A legendary location is only good when you can reach the check repeatedly without wasting half the inventory on the way there.
image_alt: All 4 Legendary Pokemon Locations guide image
answer: The four legendary targets need different route plans: Flamexor in fire-route preparation, Voltscale through tempo routes, Shadowclaw through ghost loops, and Primordion as a late-game target. Scout first, then spend Lucky Charm only on repeatable checks.
steps: Choose one legendary target before planning the route.
Use Volcanic Cave-style preparation for Flamexor.
Use Thunder Arena tempo planning for Voltscale.
Use a short Shadow Marsh loop for Shadowclaw.
Treat Primordion as a late-game route project.
Scout the location without Lucky Charm first.
Use Lucky Charm only when the legendary check is repeatable.
If the route consumes too much recovery, improve the path before spending more buffs.
recommended_setup: Flamexor: fire pressure and survival support.
Voltscale: speed, tempo, and clean arena routing.
Shadowclaw: short ghost-route loops with status control.
Primordion: late-game team planning with strong backup support.
Recipe: Lucky Charm for repeatable checks, not blind exploration.
Best use: players choosing which legendary route is realistic for their current progress.
common_mistakes: Treating every legendary route as the same plan.
Using Lucky Charm before reaching the check consistently.
Chasing multiple targets without learning one location.
Ignoring travel and recovery cost.
Farming Primordion too early because it sounds important.
Blaming bad luck when the route itself is inefficient.

faqs.question: What makes legendary location checks expensive?
faqs.answer: They become expensive when the target changes every run. Pick one legendary, one habitat, and one support plan before spending Lucky Charm.

faqs.question: Which legendary should I target first?
faqs.answer: Target the one tied to the route you can repeat most cleanly, not necessarily the flashiest name.

faqs.question: Should Lucky Charm be saved for one legendary?
faqs.answer: Yes. Pick one target and one route first. Lucky Charm performs best when it supports a repeatable legendary window.

faqs.question: Are all legendary routes similar?
faqs.answer: No. Flamexor, Voltscale, Shadowclaw, and Primordion each need different preparation.

faqs.question: What if a legendary route feels too expensive?
faqs.answer: Scout more cheaply, shorten the route, or choose a target that better matches your current team.

faqs.question: Should I rotate targets often?
faqs.answer: No. Pick one target and build enough attempts to learn the route properly.

faqs.question: How should I compare legendary routes?
faqs.answer: Compare routes by access cost, repeatability, and support pressure. The best target is the one your team can check cleanly.

faqs.question: When should I stop rotating legendary targets?
faqs.answer: Stop rotating when you have not learned any single route well enough to repeat the target window.

title: Crystal Cave Discovery Guide
content:
Crystal Cave is a discovery route with resource value. It rewards careful branch selection and punishes players who spend Lucky Charm before knowing where the meaningful checks are. Crystion-style teams do best when the route is planned, not when every path is explored equally.

Crystion is the natural anchor for crystal and Fairy/Crystal value. Crystalwing is useful when the route asks for more mobility or late-branch pressure. Lucky Charm belongs on repeated hidden or rare checks, while Mega Restore is better for long exploration attempts where one mistake can end the run.

The first visit should answer one question: which part of the cave is worth repeating? Once you know that, the route becomes a focused loop instead of a wandering full clear.
image_alt: Crystal Cave Discovery Guide guide image
answer: Crystal Cave should be scouted as a discovery route, then farmed as a focused loop. Use Crystion for crystal value, Crystalwing for later pressure, and Lucky Charm only on repeated hidden or rare checks.
steps: Scout the cave once without Lucky Charm.
Identify which branch contains the useful crystal, hidden, or rare value.
Use Crystion when Fairy/Crystal value matters.
Add Crystalwing when later branches need mobility or pressure.
Use Mega Restore for long exploration attempts if mistakes are costly.
Use Lucky Charm only after the hidden or rare check is repeatable.
Cut branches that do not support the target.
Turn the cave into a focused loop before farming it seriously.
recommended_setup: Anchor: Crystion for crystal-focused value.
Pressure option: Crystalwing for deeper branches.
Support: durable backup for longer exploration.
Recipe: Lucky Charm for repeated hidden checks; Mega Restore for long attempts.
Route style: scout, identify value, then repeat the useful branch.
Best use: players farming crystal resources or hidden cave checks.
common_mistakes: Using Lucky Charm before finding the right room.
Clearing every branch every time.
Ignoring that Crystal Cave is about route knowledge as much as team strength.
Forgetting recovery support on long exploration attempts.
Leaving Crystion out of crystal-focused routes.
Calling the cave inefficient before shortening the path.

faqs.question: What is Crystal Cave best for?
faqs.answer: It is best for crystal resources, hidden checks, and discovery-style route planning.

faqs.question: Should I use Lucky Charm on the first visit?
faqs.answer: No. Scout first, then use Lucky Charm only when the check is repeatable.

faqs.question: Which Pokemon should I use?
faqs.answer: Crystion is the main anchor. Crystalwing helps when deeper branches need pressure or mobility.

faqs.question: When should I use Mega Restore?
faqs.answer: Use it for long exploration attempts where one mistake can end the run.

faqs.question: Should I full clear the cave?
faqs.answer: Not for farming. Find the valuable branch and repeat that loop.

faqs.question: What makes Crystal Cave confusing?
faqs.answer: Crystal Cave becomes confusing when every branch is treated as equal. Scout first, then repeat the branch with the best crystal or rare-check value.

faqs.question: How should I scout Crystal Cave?
faqs.answer: Use one low-cost visit to mark branches, hidden checks, and exit points before spending Lucky Charm or Mega Restore.

faqs.question: When should I stop exploring and start farming?
faqs.answer: Start farming when one branch clearly produces the target material or Pokemon check more reliably than the full cave.

title: Best Grass-Type Pick for Every Team
content:
Grass picks are strongest when they support stable farming rather than chasing raw damage. Thornvine gives simple pressure, Leafon adds better control for longer routes, and Tropius is useful when flying-style movement or broader support matters. The best grass pick depends on the route you are trying to make easier.

Forest Valley is the natural testing ground because it shows whether the grass pick helps with food, early captures, and safe repeat attempts. Later routes may ask for more control or mobility, which is where Leafon and Tropius start to matter more.

Do not judge grass Pokemon only by damage. A good grass pick should reduce failed runs, improve farming comfort, or cover a route problem that your main carry cannot solve.
image_alt: Best Grass-Type Pick for Every Team guide image
answer: The best grass pick depends on the route: Thornvine for simple pressure, Leafon for longer control routes, and Tropius when broader support or flying-style value matters. Choose the one that makes the next route easier.
steps: Choose the route problem before choosing the grass Pokemon.
Use Thornvine when you need simple grass pressure and beginner farming value.
Use Leafon when longer routes need control and sustain.
Use Tropius when mobility or broader support matters.
Test grass picks in Forest Valley before moving into harder routes.
Pair grass picks with coverage for fire or flying pressure.
Use Grass Heal when survival is the bottleneck, not when damage is the issue.
Keep the grass slot if it improves route comfort, even if it is not the highest damage pick.
recommended_setup: Beginner pressure: Thornvine for simple farming routes.
Control route: Leafon for longer grass-poison style value.
Support option: Tropius when mobility or flying overlap matters.
Recipe: Grass Heal when a route needs sustain.
Test area: Forest Valley for early grass-route evaluation.
Best use: farming comfort, route control, and safe support around a stronger carry.
common_mistakes: Choosing grass picks only by damage.
Ignoring fire or flying pressure in backup planning.
Dropping a useful support pick because it is not flashy.
Using Grass Heal when the problem is slow damage, not survival.
Skipping Forest Valley testing before harder routes.
Forcing one grass Pokemon into every team.

faqs.question: Who is the best grass Pokemon?
faqs.answer: Thornvine is simple and practical, Leafon is better for control, and Tropius adds broader support. The best pick depends on the route.

faqs.question: Is Thornvine only for beginners?
faqs.answer: No. Thornvine remains useful when simple grass pressure is enough to stabilize farming.

faqs.question: When should I use Leafon?
faqs.answer: Use Leafon when the route rewards control, sustain, or grass-poison overlap.

faqs.question: What does Tropius add?
faqs.answer: Tropius is useful when the team needs broader support or flying-style route value.

faqs.question: Should I use Grass Heal?
faqs.answer: Use Grass Heal when survival is the bottleneck, not as a default button.

faqs.question: Can Grass rankings change?
faqs.answer: Yes. Grass value changes when Forest Valley routes, healing needs, or poison-side matchups become more or less important.

faqs.question: Should I always choose the strongest Grass pick?
faqs.answer: Choose the Grass Pokemon that fixes your route. A defensive or healing pick can outperform a stronger attacker when the run fails through survival.

faqs.question: Are Grass picks easy to farm?
faqs.answer: Many Grass routes are beginner-friendly, but rare Grass targets still need weather, food, and route timing checks.

title: Steel-Type Hard-Core Build Guide
content:
Steel teams should feel sturdy, but they still need a reason to exist on the route. Mechabit gives utility, Bronzorm adds bulk, and Ironclaw is the pressure option when steel damage needs to matter. The best steel team is not the slowest team; it is the team that absorbs pressure while keeping the clear moving.

Steel Shell is the obvious recipe, but it should be used with intention. If the route already survives, another layer of defense may only slow progress. Use Steel Shell when it protects a mining loop, hard room, or repeated attempt that would otherwise fail.

Steel teams are especially useful in routes where random damage or long fights ruin consistency. They are less useful when the goal is pure speed or when the route asks for a different matchup entirely.
image_alt: Steel-Type Hard-Core Build Guide guide image
answer: A good steel build uses Mechabit for utility, Bronzorm for bulk, and Ironclaw for pressure. Steel Shell should protect a specific hard section, not turn every route into a slow defensive clear.
steps: Use Mechabit when utility and resistance matter more than raw damage.
Add Bronzorm when the route needs heavier bulk.
Use Ironclaw when steel pressure must help finish fights.
Test whether the route needs defense or faster clears before using Steel Shell.
Use Steel Shell for a hard room, mining loop, or repeated attempt that fails without it.
Keep one damage slot so the team does not become too slow.
Avoid steel builds on routes where the matchup does not help.
After failures, check whether the issue was survival, damage, or route fit.
recommended_setup: Utility: Mechabit for flexible steel support.
Bulk: Bronzorm when long fights need durability.
Pressure: Ironclaw when the team needs steel damage.
Recipe: Steel Shell for known danger sections.
Route fit: mining loops, hard rooms, and consistency-focused clears.
Best use: players who need durability without losing all tempo.
common_mistakes: Building steel teams with no finishing power.
Using Steel Shell when the route already survives easily.
Forcing steel into matchups where its resistance does not matter.
Ignoring Ironclaw when pressure is the missing piece.
Making every clear safe but too slow to farm.
Replacing the whole team instead of balancing bulk and damage.

faqs.question: What is the best steel team core?
faqs.answer: Mechabit, Bronzorm, and Ironclaw cover utility, bulk, and pressure.

faqs.question: When does Steel Shell support steel teams?
faqs.answer: Use Steel Shell when the steel team needs to survive one dangerous section while keeping enough damage to finish the route.

faqs.question: Are steel teams slow?
faqs.answer: They can be if built poorly. A good steel team keeps enough pressure to finish fights.

faqs.question: Where do steel teams work best?
faqs.answer: They work best in hard rooms, mining loops, and routes where survival protects repeat attempts.

faqs.question: Should every hard route use steel?
faqs.answer: No. Use steel when resistance and durability solve the actual route problem.

faqs.question: What is the biggest mistake in Electric/Steel team builds?
faqs.answer: Filling every slot with Electric/Steel type Pokemon instead of covering type weaknesses. A good electric/steel team needs defensive backup, utility roles, and coverage for resistances that pure Electric/Steel typing cannot handle. Check the related habitat pages for Pokemon that complement your core without breaking the type theme.

faqs.question: What recipes work best with Electric/Steel teams?
faqs.answer: Electric/Steel teams work best with recipes that boost the team's primary role. Damage-oriented Electric/Steel teams benefit from burst or damage buff recipes. Defensive teams need sustain and armor recipes. Check the recipe page for buffs that align with your team's specific role composition.

faqs.question: How many Electric/Steel Pokemon do I need before starting this build?
faqs.answer: Start the build when you have 3 confirmed Electric/Steel Pokemon with different roles (Tank, Attacker, Support or similar). The remaining slots should cover type weaknesses and provide utility. Commit to a full electric/steel build only after the core is stable.

title: Fairy Glen Hidden Secrets
content:
Fairy Glen is an exploration route, not a straight-line combat test. Its value comes from hidden checks, side paths, and knowing which parts of the area are worth repeating. Rushing the main path usually misses the point of the habitat.

Crystion is a strong anchor because Fairy/Crystal value fits the area well. Mysticat and Magicalure help when the route asks for more fairy-style pressure or hidden-check consistency. Lucky Charm should wait until you know the repeatable hidden route; using it on the first visit is usually wasteful.

The right way to farm Fairy Glen is to scout once, mark the meaningful checks, then repeat the shortest route that touches them. Treat it like a discovery loop, not a boss corridor.
image_alt: Fairy Glen Hidden Secrets guide image
answer: Fairy Glen rewards careful exploration and hidden-check routing. Use Crystion as the anchor, add Mysticat or Magicalure for fairy pressure, and save Lucky Charm until the hidden route is repeatable.
steps: Scout Fairy Glen once without Lucky Charm.
Mark the hidden checks or side paths that actually matter.
Use Crystion when Fairy/Crystal coverage fits the route.
Add Mysticat or Magicalure when fairy pressure improves consistency.
Skip main-path rushing if hidden checks are the real target.
Use Lucky Charm only after the hidden-check route is repeatable.
Keep one support slot for safer exploration.
Repeat the shortest route that touches the valuable checks.
recommended_setup: Anchor: Crystion for Fairy/Crystal value.
Fairy pressure: Mysticat or Magicalure depending on route needs.
Support: one safer backup for exploration mistakes.
Recipe: Lucky Charm for repeated hidden checks.
Route style: scout, mark checks, repeat the useful path.
Best use: players looking for hidden value rather than pure combat clears.
common_mistakes: Rushing the main path and missing hidden checks.
Using Lucky Charm before learning the route.
Treating Fairy Glen as pure combat.
Clearing every branch after the valuable checks are already known.
Ignoring support because the area does not look hard at first.
Switching targets before testing the same hidden loop enough times.

faqs.question: What is Fairy Glen best for?
faqs.answer: It is best for hidden checks, Fairy/Crystal value, and careful exploration loops.

faqs.question: Should I use Lucky Charm immediately?
faqs.answer: No. Use it only after the hidden route is known and repeatable.

faqs.question: Which Pokemon should I bring?
faqs.answer: Crystion is the anchor, while Mysticat or Magicalure can add fairy-style pressure.

faqs.question: Is Fairy Glen a hard route?
faqs.answer: It is not the hardest route, but it rewards attention. Rushing can make it feel low value.

faqs.question: Should I full clear Fairy Glen?
faqs.answer: Only while scouting. For farming, repeat the shortest route that reaches the valuable hidden checks.

faqs.question: What makes Fairy Glen attempts messy?
faqs.answer: Fairy Glen gets messy when hidden checks are chased before the team can handle the route safely. Stabilize the path before using Lucky Charm.

faqs.question: How should I approach Fairy Glen first?
faqs.answer: Treat the first visit as mapping. Identify the hidden section, then return with a recipe only when the path is repeatable.

faqs.question: When should I use a shorter Fairy Glen loop?
faqs.answer: Use a shorter loop when full clears add more risk than hidden-check value.

title: Nightmare Forest Horror Stories
content:
Nightmare Forest is a pressure route with a dramatic name, but the danger is practical: long fights, control problems, poison or darkness pressure, and expensive failed attempts. Treat it like a hard habitat, not a story stroll.

Leafon helps with grass-poison control, Frostbite can support harder sections, and Magicalure gives value when the route overlaps with fairy or late-route pressure. Ghost Veil should be saved for the window where the route becomes dangerous, while Steel Shell is better if the issue is survival rather than ghost-style pressure.

The safest plan is to scout cheaply, identify the section that breaks the run, then bring the right defensive or control recipe. Rare farming should wait until the normal route is stable enough to repeat.
image_alt: Nightmare Forest Horror Stories guide image
answer: Nightmare Forest is a hard control route. Use Leafon for grass-poison pressure, Frostbite or Magicalure for support, and save Ghost Veil or Steel Shell for the section that actually breaks the run.
steps: Reach the required progress before treating Nightmare Forest as a serious route.
Scout once without rare buffs to find the dangerous section.
Use Leafon when grass-poison control helps manage pressure.
Add Frostbite or Magicalure depending on whether the route needs durability or fairy-style support.
Use Ghost Veil if ghost or darkness pressure is the problem.
Use Steel Shell if survival is failing more than damage control.
Do not rare farm until normal clears are stable.
Shorten the route around the valuable check once the danger section is understood.
recommended_setup: Control: Leafon for grass-poison pressure.
Support: Frostbite for harder sections or Magicalure for fairy-style value.
Recipe: Ghost Veil for ghost/dark pressure; Steel Shell for survival failures.
Backup: one sustain or durability option for long fights.
Route style: cheap scout, identify danger, then run a focused clear.
Best use: late-game players preparing hard control routes and rare checks.
common_mistakes: Entering because the name sounds like story content instead of a hard route.
Using only burst damage with no sustain.
Spending Ghost Veil before finding the dangerous section.
Trying to rare farm before normal clears are stable.
Ignoring whether the failure is control, survival, or route length.
Full-clearing when a shorter focused loop would be safer.

faqs.question: What makes Nightmare Forest dangerous?
faqs.answer: Nightmare Forest punishes teams that enter for rare checks before they can handle darkness pressure. Build survival before rare farming.

faqs.question: Is Nightmare Forest hard?
faqs.answer: Yes. It should be treated as a hard control route with pressure, sustain, and route-planning demands.

faqs.question: Which Pokemon should I bring?
faqs.answer: Leafon is useful for grass-poison control, while Frostbite or Magicalure can support harder sections.

faqs.question: When is Ghost Veil best in Nightmare Forest?
faqs.answer: Use Ghost Veil when the team can already reach the dark section and needs protection for the key ghost-heavy room.

faqs.question: When is Steel Shell better?
faqs.answer: Use Steel Shell when the route fails because of survival pressure rather than ghost-style control.

faqs.question: Should I rare farm immediately?
faqs.answer: No. Make normal clears stable first, then shorten the route around the valuable check.

faqs.question: How should I test Nightmare Forest?
faqs.answer: Run a short survival check first. If the team reaches the dark section cleanly, then test Ghost Veil or Steel Shell timing.

faqs.question: When should I stop rare farming there?
faqs.answer: Stop when every rare attempt depends on emergency recovery. The route needs a stronger support plan before more farming.

title: Late-Game Team Planning Guide
content:
Late-game teams should be frameworks, not copied lineups. Start with the carry that fits the target route, add one defensive or sustain anchor, then use the final slot for speed, coverage, or utility. The strongest names in the database still need a route that lets them work.

Flamexor fits fire pressure and boss finishing, Shadowclaw belongs in ghost-heavy rare routes, Voltscale brings tempo and electric-dragon value, and Primordion should be treated as a late-game anchor rather than a shortcut. Recipes should change with the route: Lucky Charm for repeatable rare checks, Steel Shell for survival, Speed Potion for clean loops, and Mega Restore for long attempts.

When an endgame team fails, resist the urge to replace everything. Identify the failing room, decide whether the problem is survival, damage, speed, or route length, and change one slot or recipe at a time.
image_alt: Late-Game Team Planning Guide guide image
answer: The best late-game build is a framework: one route-specific carry, one defensive or sustain anchor, and one speed, coverage, or utility slot. Flamexor, Shadowclaw, Voltscale, and Primordion all need different support.
steps: Choose the target habitat before choosing the carry.
Use Flamexor when fire pressure or boss finishing matters.
Use Shadowclaw for ghost-heavy rare routes.
Use Voltscale when tempo and electric-dragon pressure matter.
Use Primordion as a late-game anchor after support routes are ready.
Add one defensive or sustain slot to keep the carry alive.
Use the third slot for speed, coverage, or utility based on the route bottleneck.
Change recipes with the objective instead of using the same buff everywhere.
After a failure, adjust one slot or recipe before rebuilding the whole team.

title: Pokémon Pokopia Guide: Block Float Underwater Building
content: Guides Home Guides Pokemon Pokopia Block Float Recipe & Unlock Gameplay Guides 2026-08-07 Pokemon Pokopia Block Float Recipe & Unlock Craft Block Floats in Pokemon Pokopia: unlock the 500-Coin recipe at Bubbly Basin Environment Level 2, use Stardust Rock and Pokémetal, then build underwater. Author : Pokopia Guide Team The Block Float is the practical building block for structures that do not touch the seafloor. It can support objects and buildings on water or underwater, making it much easier to create suspended rooms, platforms, and underwater houses without first constructing a pillar from the ground. Block Float Recipe and Unlock Requirement Detail Recipe source Bubbly Basin shop Shop unlock Bubbly Basin Environment Level 2 Recipe price 500 Coins Crafting material Stardust Rock ×1 Crafting material Pokémetal ×1 Raise Bubbly Basin to Environment Level 2 before looking for the recipe. The shop will then sell it for 500 Coins. Craft each Block Float with one Stardust Rock and one Pokémetal . What a Block Float Does Use a Block Float as a temporary or permanent foothold in water. It is useful whenever the structure you want to place has no contact with the ground. The item description specifically identifies it as a float for building on or under water and for making objects float. The important rule is that blocks placed on top of a Block Float remain in place after the Block Float is removed . You do not need to leave a large number of floats inside the finished build. A few floats are enough to establish the first layer; remove or relocate them once the rest of the structure is placed. How to Build Underwater with Block Floats Learn Dive and bring the Block Floats to the desired depth. Place one at the height where you want to start the structure. Place normal blocks or objects on and around the float to make the first platform. Extend the platform and build walls, floors, or a house as usual. Remove the temporary float when the placed blocks are stable, then reuse it for another section. This method is most helpful when building far above the seafloor. A ground-to-platform pillar still works, but it takes more blocks and is slower to remove afterward. Plan the First Layer Before You Place It The first layer is the part of a suspended build that determines everything above it. Decide the floor height and footprint before spending materials on walls or decoration. For a small room, place one float near the center, make a compact floor around it, then expand outward. For a wider platform, establish several points across the planned footprint before joining them with regular blocks. This avoids discovering too late that one edge sits at the wrong height. Keep the floats accessible while working. A float that is completely enclosed by walls, furniture, or a finished floor is harder to recover. Treat it as temporary scaffolding: build the usable first layer, remove the float, then finish the visual details. This is also useful when testing an underwater design, since you can reposition the same material rather than committing to a permanent support layout. Where Block Floats Work Best Block Floats are not only for a full underwater house. They are practical for a small observation deck above the bottom, a bridge-like route between raised sections, a furniture display set at water level, or a room that you want to look suspended inside a larger underwater build. They work best when the desired starting point has no natural surface nearby. For simple ground-level decoration, building directly on the seafloor is usually quicker. Save Block Floats for designs where their ability to start in open water removes a real constraint. Carry several on a long Dive trip, but do not overcraft them: the same float can be collected and moved after each first layer is complete. Block Floats vs. Construction Kits Construction Kits can be placed without first making a block foothold. Use them when the building itself has a kit and you only need to place the finished structure. Use Block Floats when you are designing a custom build block by block, placing furniture at a chosen height, or making an underwater platform before adding details. Situation Better choice Place a premade building kit Construction Kit Build a custom underwater room Block Float Add a floating furniture platform Block Float Reach a very high underwater point Block Float Common Mistakes Looking for the recipe before Environment Level 2 The recipe is not in the initial Bubbly Basin shop inventory. Raise Environment Level first, then return with 500 Coins. Treating every Block Float as permanent support Blocks placed on top stay after the float is destroyed. Recover the float after setting the structure's first layer instead of crafting one for every tile. Building from the seafloor by default Pillars from the ground remain a valid method, but Block Floats are faster when the target is high above the bottom or when you want a clean suspended design. Forgetting to bring materials before a long Dive The recipe is cheap per float, but the useful building materials are the blocks and furnishings placed afterward. Bring the planned floor blocks, a few spare floats, and any furniture before heading deep into Bubbly Basin. Returning to restock is possible, but it interrupts a build more than preparing the first layer on shore. title: Pokémon Pokopia Multiplayer Guide
content: Guides Home Guides Pokopia Multiplayer Guide: Co-op & Modes Gameplay Guides 2026-03-19 Pokopia Multiplayer Guide: Co-op & Modes Multiplayer guide for Pokemon Pokopia. Host and join, Palette Town vs Cloud Island vs Guest Mode, couch co-op, unlock at Env. Level 2, host vs guest item rules. Author : Pokopia Guide Team Find multiplayer partners on Discord Use the community server for co-op partners, trades, and multiplayer help. Join our Discord How to Play Multiplayer Playing as a Host Select " Play via Communications " from the PC in the Pokémon Center. Select " Invite others to your town ". Choose either Internet Communication or Local Communication (Internet requires a Nintendo Switch Online membership). Configure the multiplayer settings and press the + Button to confirm. When playing in towns other than Palette Town, it will be in Visit Mode only, and moves or items cannot be used. Shared Play is for Palette Town only Multiplayer using Shared Play can only be done in Palette Town . If you want to play in "Palette Town" The host should move through the map to Palette Town. The guest does not need to move there themselves. When the host moves to a different town, a confirmation prompt will appear for the guest. Playing as a Guest Select " Play via Communication " from the PC in the Pokémon Center Select " Visit a friend's town " For Internet communication, enter the Link Code (shared by the host) Confirm the destination and select it Types of Multiplayer Features of Each Multiplayer Mode Type Features Palette Town Can build together, shared play supported, guests cannot take items back Cloud Island Can build even when the host is away, viewing only is also possible in Virtual Mode, items cannot be taken back (Host can only learn recipes) Guest Mode (Story Towns) Viewing only, set in towns visited during the story Recommendations by Playstyle Purpose Recommendation Build together (Shared Play) Palette Town Build together (Host offline OK) Cloud Island Show your story town Guest Mode Explore Cloud Island freely Virtual Mode What You Can Do in Multiplayer Build on Cloud Island Cloud Island is a multiplayer island where you can progress with town building even when the host is away. Up to 4 players can play simultaneously, and since there is no limit on players swapping in and out, many players can participate. You cannot take Pokémon or items back with you (applies to both hosts and guests). Building in Palette Town Palette Town is a place where you can enjoy building your town freely. Up to 4 players can play together at once, and all participants can contribute to town-building by placing blocks and more. Only the host can take back Pokemon and items. Guests cannot. View Towns in Spectator Mode Multiplayer in towns other than Fresh Town will be in Spectator Mode. Guests cannot use moves or items. Invite Pokemon to Your Town If you talk to a Pokemon in the host's town twice, you can select "Come visit my place next time." If you give a "Star Piece" to a visiting Pokemon, you will receive a "Souvenir." Opening the souvenir in an empty habitat will make a Pokemon of the same species appear. Take Commemorative Photos During multiplayer, you can enjoy taking commemorative photos with other players using the in-game camera function. You can also take selfies using the in-camera mode. Multiplayer Unlock Conditions It is unlocked by raising the Environment Level of the Withered Wastelands to 2 . This can be reached in about 1 hour from the start of the game. Differences Between Host and Guest Item Host Guest Bring back Pokemon ○ (Fresh Town only) ✕ Bring back items ○ (Fresh Town only) ✕ Bring back from Cloud Island ✕ (Recipe acquisition only) ✕ Management functions (Town travel/Settings) ○ ✕ On Cloud Island, neither the host nor the guest can bring back Pokemon or items. Only the host can acquire recipes. Previous Gameplay Guides Pokopia Ditto Moves: All 14 & Upgrades Next Gameplay Guides Pokopia Paint Guide: All Colors & Smearguru Found incorrect data? title: Pokémon Pokopia Mystery Gift Codes Guide
content: Guides Home Guides Pokopia Mystery Gift Codes & How to Redeem About Pokopia 2026-06-16 Pokopia Mystery Gift Codes & How to Redeem All active Pokémon Pokopia Mystery Gift serial codes and how to redeem them. Free furniture, materials, and decorations, plus where every code comes from and its deadline. Author : Pokopia Guide Team _Last updated: June 16, 2026 — codes and deadlines verified as of this date._ Mystery Gift (ふしぎなおくりもの) lets you claim free in-game rewards in Pokémon Pokopia — furniture, materials, and decorations. Some are claimed straight over the internet, others need a serial code from an official source. This guide lists the active codes, every current gift, and exactly how to redeem them. Note: Most Pokopia rewards come from official channels (guidebooks, CoroCoro Comic, campaigns, store bonuses) rather than universal codes. Codes and deadlines change over time — always confirm in-game. Active Serial Code Code Reward Deadline `P0K0P1AGARDENS` Lucky Tree (plant furniture) October 7, 2026 Enter it exactly as shown in the Mystery Gift menu (see steps below). How to Redeem Mystery Gifts Before you start, you need a Nintendo Account linked to the user account that will receive the gift, and an internet connection. Play until the PC is unlocked (about 30 minutes in, after the challenge intro) Enter a Pokémon Center and interact with the blue PC at the back right Select "Receive Items" (アイテムを受け取る) Choose "Mystery Gift" (ふしぎなおくりもの) Pick your method: Receive via Internet — for gifts distributed online (no code needed) Receive via Serial Code — type in a code like the one above The game auto-saves when the gift is delivered All Current Gifts Gift Contents How to Get Deadline Lucky Tree Plant furniture Serial code `P0K0P1AGARDENS` Oct 7, 2026 Ditto Rug Decoration Receive via Internet (early-purchase bonus) Jan 31, 2027 Monsterball Set 3 furniture pieces CoroCoro Comic May issue Jul 12, 2026 Munch Munch Set Berries ×2, Fresh Carrot ×2, Beans ×2 "Like" the official Pokémon X post Feb 28, 2027 Flat Tree Plant furniture Amazon limited edition packaging Jan 31, 2027 Crafting Support Set Building materials Official Start Book (¥1,980) Mar 5, 2027 Rare Pokemetal ×30 Rare crafting material Expansion Pass purchase bonus Aug 31, 2027 Several of these items (like the Ditto Rug and the plant trees) can also be obtained through normal gameplay if you miss the distribution. Where Codes Come From There is no universal "everyone can use" code list for Pokopia. Serial codes are tied to specific official sources: Official Pokémon X (Twitter) campaigns — like/repost rewards with reply codes CoroCoro Comic monthly issues Official guidebooks (e.g. the Start Book) Store-exclusive bonuses (Amazon limited editions, etc.) Expansion Pass purchase bonuses Tips Redeem before deadlines — many gifts expire in 2026–2027; claim them early Link your Nintendo Account first — gifts won't deliver without it Check official channels — follow the official Pokémon X account for new campaign codes Don't worry if you miss one — several reward items are also obtainable through normal play Previous About Pokopia Pokopia DLC FAQ: Bubbly Basin, Dive & Expansion Pass Next Resources & How to Get How to Make Concrete in Pokémon Pokopia: Mixer & Limestone Found incorrect data? content: Guides Home Guides Pokopia DLC FAQ: Bubbly Basin, Dive & Expansion Pass About Pokopia 2026-08-05 Pokopia DLC FAQ: Bubbly Basin, Dive & Expansion Pass Current Pokemon Pokopia DLC FAQ: free Ver. 2.0.0 Dive update, Bubbly Basin entry route through Manaphy and the Master-rank gate, Expansion Pass access, and price. Author : Pokopia Guide Team Part 1 of the Pokemon Pokopia Expansion Pass, Bubbly Basin , is live. The same release delivered the free Ver. 2.0.0 update, including Dive, underwater exploration, and underwater building. Quick Answers Question Answer Is Dive free? Yes. It is part of the free Ver. 2.0.0 update. Is Bubbly Basin paid? Yes. It is Expansion Pass Part 1. How do I learn Dive? Complete Manaphy's Bleak Beach request: bring it 5 Seaweed, then collect the Poke Ball Ornament underwater. What opens the DLC gate? Dive to the western Bleak Beach seafloor gate and present the Pokedex with Master Trainer Rank . Do I need the Ditto Flag? No, but it is recommended so you can establish a base and use Home Navigator. What does the pass cost? Nintendo US lists all three parts together for US$34.99 ; regional stores vary. The Actual Entry Route The previous pre-release requirement list is no longer current. The verified in-game route is: Talk to Tangrowth at the Bleak Beach Pokemon Center. Reach Manaphy's northwest island with Surf. Bring Manaphy 5 Seaweed, learn Dive, collect the Poke Ball Ornament underwater, and finish the request. Talk to Popplio at the Pokemon Center. Dive to the depression on the western seafloor, then open the gate with Master Trainer Rank. See the full Bubbly Basin DLC guide for the route, Environment Level 3 objective, Sea Temple, and Pokemon-specific progression. Free Update vs. Expansion Pass Free Ver. 2.0.0 update Requires Expansion Pass Part 1 Dive, underwater exploration, and underwater building Bubbly Basin town access Underwater gameplay improvements DLC-town furniture, Ditto outfits, and Pokemon content The DLC Pokédex has 50 numbers and 52 form records . Their habitats, required materials, rarities, specialties, favorites, and environment preferences are listed in this site's Pokédex and habitat database. Expansion Pass Schedule Part Status Part 1 Available now: Bubbly Basin Part 2 Planned for late 2026 Part 3 Planned for 2027 The three parts are sold together as one Expansion Pass, not individually. title: Pokémon Pokopia Smoothie Guide
content: Guides Home Guides Pokemon Pokopia Smoothies: Mixer Unlock, All Recipes, and Underwater Surf Gameplay Guides 2026-08-07 Pokemon Pokopia Smoothies: Mixer Unlock, All Recipes, and Underwater Surf Make Smoothies in Pokemon Pokopia with Cut Watermelon and two ingredients. Unlock the Mixer through Mudkip's Bubbly Basin request, use Surf while Diving, and check all six known Smoothie recipes and offering effects. Author : Pokopia Guide Team Smoothies are the key food for faster underwater travel in Bubbly Basin. Drink one to use Surf while Diving : Ditto turns into Lapras and can move through the sea more quickly. Every known recipe begins with Cut Watermelon , so prepare Watermelon Seeds and a Pokemon with the Cut Trees specialty before you unlock the Mixer. Unlock the Mixer The Mixer is a reward from a Mudkip request that appears after completing the Bubbly Basin story. Once it is available, put Cut Watermelon and two other ingredients into the Mixer to make a Smoothie. Whole Watermelon does not substitute for Cut Watermelon. Give Watermelon to a Pokemon with the Cut Trees specialty first. See Watermelon and Cut Watermelon: Locations and Uses for the seed unlock and processing route. Why Smoothies Matter Drinking any Smoothie upgrades Surf during Dive. It is valuable when you are repeatedly crossing Bubbly Basin, entering long caves, or collecting materials around the underwater town. While boosted Surf is active, you can dash underwater and use Whirlpool to break blocks by holding ZR. Prepare a Smoothie before leaving a convenient Mixer instead of waiting until you are already deep underwater. Known Smoothie Recipes Smoothie Ingredients Offering effect Watermelon Smoothie Cut Watermelon + two ingredients that do not make another dish Ancient items appear somewhat more often Sea Grapes Smoothie Cut Watermelon + Sea Grapes + one ingredient Ho-Oh and Lugia appear somewhat more often Leppa Smoothie Cut Watermelon + Leppa Berry + one ingredient Ancient items appear somewhat more often Red Hot Smoothie Cut Watermelon + Ripe Carrot + one ingredient; requires a Burn-specialty Pokemon Pokemon appear in habitats somewhat more often Refreshing Soda Smoothie Cut Watermelon + Soda Pop + Aspear Berry Better shop stock appears much more often Coffee Parfait Smoothie Cut Watermelon + Moomoo Milk Coffee + any bread Rare items are found much more often The last column applies when the Smoothie is offered. Recipe ingredients should be checked before mixing: a flexible slot can accept an ingredient that does not turn the result into a different dish. Cut Watermelon Is the Ingredient to Stockpile The main bottleneck is usually not the Mixer itself but maintaining enough Cut Watermelon. Watermelon has to be grown and then processed by a Pokemon with the Cut Trees specialty before it becomes usable in a Smoothie. Keep a small reserve after harvesting rather than immediately using every piece, especially once you start planning longer Dive routes. The other two slots determine which named Smoothie you make. A basic Watermelon Smoothie is the economical option when you only need underwater Surf, because it can use flexible ingredients such as Leaves. Named recipes are worth saving for a specific offering target. This keeps valuable ingredients from being used just for movement when a cheaper Smoothie would give the same Dive and Surf access. Drinking a Smoothie and Offering One Are Different Decisions Drink a Smoothie when the immediate goal is underwater travel. Its direct benefit is Surf while Diving, which helps with a long cave, repeated travel through Bubbly Basin, or a material route that would otherwise take several slow trips. Offer a Smoothie when you want the recipe's listed secondary effect. For example, Sea Grapes Smoothie is the relevant choice when pursuing Ho-Oh or Lugia, while Refreshing Soda is the one to reserve for better shop stock. The movement benefit is shared by all Smoothies, so the special ingredients only need to be spent when the offering effect is part of your plan. Before You Start a Deep Route Check four things before leaving the town: you have learned Dive, you have Cut Watermelon rather than whole Watermelon, you have made the Smoothie you intend to drink, and you have not accidentally spent a rare named-recipe ingredient meant for an offering. That short check avoids the common problem of reaching a distant cave entrance with a whole Watermelon or an empty Mixer inventory. Efficient Smoothie Preparation Reach Bubbly Basin Environment Level 2 and buy Watermelon Seeds. Grow Watermelon, then ask a Cut Trees-specialty Pokemon to make Cut Watermelon. Finish the Bubbly Basin story and Mudkip's request to obtain the Mixer. Make several Smoothies before a long Dive route. Keep special ingredients such as Sea Grapes, Leppa Berries, Psy Soda, and Moomoo Milk for the offering effects you want. Choosing a Recipe Make a basic Watermelon Smoothie when the only goal is underwater Surf and you do not want to spend rare ingredients. Choose Sea Grapes Smoothie when looking for Ho-Oh or Lugia, and use the other named recipes when their offering bonus matches your current goal. The Mixer is also a reason not to process just one Watermelon at a time: a small reserve of Cut Watermelon lets you react to the ingredient you find. Smoothie FAQ Can I Surf while Diving without a Smoothie? No. The Smoothie is the confirmed item that enables Surf during Dive. Why does the Mixer reject my Watermelon? The recipe needs Cut Watermelon . Process the whole fruit through a Pokemon with the Cut Trees specialty. Do all Smoothies improve underwater movement? Yes. The named recipes all upgrade Surf while Diving; their ingredient differences determine the offering effect.
